newsitem.title: USA: Term-limited Wash. lawmakers sue to save jobs.
newsitem.headline: Term-limited Wash. lawmakers sue to save jobs.

text.p: Six Washington state legislators filed suit in the state Supreme Court Friday challenging voter-approved limits on their terms in office.
National term limit advocates predicted the challenge would fail as have similar lawsuits by endangered politicians in California, Maine and Arkansas.

"State limits have been upheld across the country," said Jonathan Ferry, spokesman for Washington, D.C.-based U.S. Term Limits. "It really just seems to be a desperate attempt by those who are going to be limited out to do an end run around the voters and to cling to the reins of power."

The six lawmakers, each backed by a voter from their district, Common Cause of Washington and the American Civil Liberties Union, signed onto the legal challenge. They seek direct review by the state Supreme Court, contending that term limits represent an unconstitutional restriction on the rights of voters and the candidacy of incumbents for state offices.

"Citizens should be able to vote for the candidates of their choice regardless of whether they are incumbents," argued state ACLU executive director Kathleen Taylor. "All candidates who meet constitutional requirements should be able to run for public office. If citizens no longer want an incumbent to serve in office, they have the right and power to vote the person out."

In 1992, Washington voters passed a citizens' initiative limiting terms in office of members of Congress, the governor, lieutenant governor and state legislators. The U.S. Supreme Court threw out the term limits on federal officials but left the state limits alone.
The law restricts state representatives to six years and state senators to eight years in office. The governor and lieutenant governor can serve no more than two terms each.
Ferry said 20 states have passed term limits on state officials by voter initiative since the early 1990s.

But one of the lawmakers filing suit against Washington state's law described term limits as a waning fad. "The worm has turned," said state Sen. Valoria Loveland, adding she has no fear of political repercussions from challenging the voters' will.
